claims.text: Matching projects treat a function as done only when compiling candidate C with the original toolchain (e.g., SGI IDO 5.3 for Mario 64) reproduces the original bytes instruction for instruction. This is stronger than behavioural equivalence: it rules out off-by-one errors, changed float precision or silently removed undefined behaviour, so a matching function is evidence the range and logic really belong together.

meta.query: How do decompilation projects recover the exact original bytes and boundaries of a function that was removed, merged or never split out of the game's executable, and what evidence do they accept that the recovered range really belongs to the function they think it does?
meta.capability: You can demand byte-identical rebuild as the acceptance test for any claimed function recovery, instead of accepting a plausible-looking reconstruction or similarity score as proof.

claims.text: A function-level match does not establish that the rebuilt file has the right literal pools, section placement or data ownership, and a checker can be fooled if it ignores referenced data or reads a stale build. Projects test their checkers with deliberately wrong candidates (changed strings, float constants, swapped pointer-table entries) and then run the full binary comparison before claiming a recovered range is correct.

meta.capability: You can stop accepting a per-function match percentage or a green checker result as proof of a correct recovery, and require that referenced data, relocations and the full linked image also match.

claims.text: Clues such as shared constants or strings, related class methods and module entry points only suggest original file boundaries. A split is accepted only if, after assigning data and rebuilding, existing matches and the final image stay intact. For overlay-based games, loader and relocation records decide which bytes belong to which function, because a plausible decompilation at the wrong address is still the wrong function.

claims.text: In a study of eight LLM decompilation systems, candidates that passed every shipped test still diverged from the original on a broader fuzzed input set 4.9% of the time overall and up to 13% for a single system. The shipped test suites missed 3% to 45% of the divergence, because their inputs sat in a narrow range and never reached edge paths like a final-band branch or integer overflow.

meta.query: Why does a recovered function that matches the original bytes sometimes still turn out to be the wrong function, for example when identical library routines or code loaded from different overlays share the same instructions, and what extra evidence do projects need to tell them apart?
meta.capability: You can stop treating 'it compiles and passes the supplied tests' as proof that recovered code is the right code, and require a wider behavioral check before accepting it.

claims.text: Cleaner-looking output can be less faithful: the strongest refinement LLM raised Ghidra's build rate from 75% to 90% while its behavioral Matched rate fell from 74% to 62%. The study attributes this to the model inventing fields, types, callees and guards where traditional tools leave visible unknowns, so errors become silent instead of obvious.

meta.capability: You can stop using build success rate as a proxy for recovery quality, and track behavioral agreement separately before paying for or trusting a 'cleaner' recovery tool.

claims.text: The distinguishing evidence is the original's actual behavior on many generated inputs, compared on return values, written bytes and global state, with divergences counted only if they reproduce across repeated runs. A separate source stresses that syntax checks only show the code parses, not that calculations or decisions are right, so project-specific tests are needed. Note the sources do not address identical library routines or overlays directly; applying this to those cases is an inference.

meta.capability: You can demand a reference-based differential check, run on the same many inputs against the original, as the evidence that separates a look-alike function from the true one, rather than relying on byte or syntax matching.

claims.text: In a documented F# compiler case (dotnet/fsharp issue #9283), a function in one library that asked 'which assembly am I running in' returned the library's own name in Debug builds but the calling application's name in Release builds, because the compiler silently copied the function's body into the caller across the library boundary. The original function boundary effectively ceased to exist in the shipped binary, and the maintainers closed the issue in 2023 without changing the behavior, so this class of silent divergence persists.

meta.query: What happens to the recovery of function boundaries when the original linker or compiler inlined, merged or reordered code, and in which real projects did the recovered split points turn out to be wrong or unverifiable?
meta.capability: You can stop assuming that a debug build and a release build of the same software behave identically, and require release-build testing before trusting anything that depends on knowing which module or function is running.

claims.text: The F# case shows boundary loss happened even though the called framework method was explicitly marked as not-inlinable, because the compiler did not honor that marking and the relevant security attribute was absent from the reference assemblies it compiled against. The maintainers' stated position was that there is no reliable attribute to detect such cases and that a maintained list of special APIs is hard to keep correct, so the only protection is the developer manually marking their own functions.

meta.query: What happens to the recovery of function boundaries when the original linker or compiler inlined, merged or reordered code, and in which real projects did the recovered split points turn out to be wrong or unverifiable?
meta.capability: You can treat the compiler's own inlining as an unmarked, undocumented change to where function boundaries sit, and require reverse-engineering or audit work on compiled binaries to assume boundaries cannot be trusted from source or declared attributes.

claims.text: Zephyr's relocation feature lets a project move code and data for whole files or libraries into different memory regions without touching the source, and it keeps relocated items from being discarded even if unused unless told otherwise. The documentation warns that relocating kernel or architecture files can break because some contain early initialization that runs before relocation takes place, so placement changes can silently alter behavior of boundary-sensitive code.

meta.query: What happens to the recovery of function boundaries when the original linker or compiler inlined, merged or reordered code, and in which real projects did the recovered split points turn out to be wrong or unverifiable?
meta.capability: You can budget for the risk that code placement is rearranged at build time by project configuration rather than by the programmers, so layout-dependent assumptions (such as which code runs before setup completes) need explicit review whenever relocation features are switched on.

claims.text: A decompilation percentage is only meaningful with its unit (functions, bytes, files, symbols, assets), its scope (whole executable, one library, a region) and the build version measured. A project with 900 of 1,000 functions matched is 90% by function count but not 90% by bytes if the remaining functions hold half the code, so the same bar can hide very different amounts of remaining work.

claims.text: An unknown progress value can mean no compatible report exists, a source was unavailable, or scope could not be established, so it does not show that no work was done. Values above 100%, shifting denominators, or conflicting badges point to a report error or differing scopes and should not be silently clamped. Code-matching and asset-identification bars should not be averaged into one completion score.

claims.text: In the Decompile-Bench pipeline, roughly 100 million raw binary functions from about 85,000 binaries were reduced to 2 million matched pairs, about 2% retained. Losses came from discarding code not defined in the project repo (system and dependency headers, trivial getters/setters), keeping only one binary function per source function (such as template instantiations), and removing near-duplicates across binaries. This is a GCC/Clang DWARF-based pipeline, not a CodeWarrior one, so it indicates the order of magnitude and the categories of unmatched code rather than a CodeWarrior count.

claims.text: Stripping removes the symbol table but leaves other structures that still enumerate functions. On the Mach-O build, a stripped file listed only one name yet a function-start list still held all five function starts in nine bytes. On Windows 64-bit images, exception-unwind entries still mark the start and end of every function that uses stack or calls another, though leaf functions are missing. A reviewer who trusts the name count will undercount badly, and the recovery methods can be scored against an unstripped twin build.

claims.text: In the worked example, an agent read a pointer slot's raw bytes and reported a call into kernel space. The word was a placeholder that the loader replaces with the real library function address before the program starts. Reading a file as if it were the running process produces confident but wrong answers, and each format (ELF, PE, Mach-O) has its own placeholder mechanism.

claims.text: Recycled routines such as initialization, encoding and networking wrappers make a binary look larger and more complex than its unique logic. Collapsing familiar code and comparing the remaining delta across samples makes the distinctive part visible. claims.text: A rebuilt function can have 46 code bytes identical to the original and an identical relocation record, yet differ in the lookup table it points at (1,2,3,4,3 versus 1,2,3,4,4). A byte comparison alone reports no change; only reading the pointed-to data catches it. This is the same failure the TH08 project documented, where source 0.0 looked exact against target 128.0 and the fix audited 1,548 literal references and corrected twelve more.

Teams chasing such a 'change' waste effort explaining something that does not exist.

Roughly 6-15MB of library code (jemalloc, zstd, Lua, curl, SDK) was therefore classed as identifiable but non-matching, and some game logic is expected never to match. The reference compiler, not the source, is what decides whether a unit can be attributed with confidence.

claims.text: Matching decompilation depends on the exact compiler, flags and source context, so a match is only valid under the configuration it was checked against. The guidance is to rebuild affected code and re-verify previously matched functions after shared types or prototypes change, and to record compiler, flags and resulting diff with each result. A late discovery that the compiler or flags were wrong therefore invalidates matches, not just the functions still open.

Teams should test their checker with deliberately wrong candidates (changed strings, constants, pointer-table entries) to confirm it rejects them, and run the full binary comparison. This reduces the chance that a hidden wrong assumption surfaces months later.

claims.text: In the Zelda: Wind Waker decomp, small residual diffs such as register swaps, out-of-order instructions or duplicated instructions can come from missing the original developers' inline functions, and debug maps from a prerelease kiosk demo are used to recover those inlines. Since inline usage changes generated code in non-obvious ways, a function forced to match with the wrong structure may be fragile, and the guide itself notes the maps only partly show inline use. This is a place where assumptions that later need revisiting accumulate.

claims.text: GitHub's Copilot matcher compares a suggestion plus roughly 150 surrounding characters against an index of public GitHub repositories only, skips edited suggestions and user-written code, and flags fewer than 1% of suggestions. The index is refreshed only every few months, so it misses new code and can point to moved or deleted files. A wrong or empty answer therefore looks clean while the real source sits outside the index or was altered after the match.

claims.text: In the March 2026 chardet case, JPlag measured structural similarity to the prior LGPL version at under 1.3%, yet the original author disputes that the rewrite is independent because the maintainer had years of access to the LGPL code and the LLM reportedly accessed metadata from that version. A near-zero similarity score can coexist with a derivative relationship, so scoring-based attribution can make a wrong 'unrelated' call look rigorous.

claims.text: Language-model tools produce confident provenance and license statements ('this is MIT', 'no copyleft') that are unsubstantiated. They are fluent enough to pass a casual review, so a wrong source or license attribution reads as plausible. The law-firm source recommends treating every non-trivial AI snippet as external third-party content to be scanned and checked.
